summary:
Meghālaya stands under India's national framework on every question that determines what a trans visitor faces: legal recognition, identity documents, entry screening, policing and remedies. Nothing in the sourced material identifies a Meghālaya-specific deviation from that national position, so the national assessment is the operative one here.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026. The measure removes the self-identification route established under the 2019 law, restricts legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner together with intersex persons, and requires medical certification of identity. Medical boards and district authorities must now certify gender-affirming surgery. The amendment reverses the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that had set self-identification as the standard, and it places trans men, trans women and non-binary people who identify outside the listed categories beyond the recognition scheme. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The amended law adds offences carrying penalties up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warned on 26 March 2026 that this provision could criminalise support networks around trans people. The government presents the narrower definition as sharpening the targeting of welfare benefits and protection from trafficking; critics, including a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel, warn that it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people. That panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling the removal of self-identification a setback to the 2014 ruling. Presidential assent remained pending in late March 2026, and Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign.

Documentation is thin in practice. Of 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, only about 32,500 hold identity cards, which leaves the large majority of recognised persons without the paper that entry checks and police encounters turn on.

The baseline for entry and stay remains mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has read to cover gender identity and sexual orientation under Article 15; the Allahabad High Court extended that reasoning to employment discrimination in 2021. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity checks remain a live point of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Assent to the March 2026 amendment was still pending in late March 2026, so the operative recognition rules for a visitor may change in either direction. A human rights organisation urged refusal of signature and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel sought withdrawal, which signals continuing contest over the scope of recognition.

The gap between the census count of 487,803 transgender persons and the roughly 32,500 identity cards issued indicates that documentation, rather than legal recognition alone, is the practical bottleneck at checkpoints.

Welfare provision varies substantially between Indian states. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha maintain transgender welfare boards with housing subsidies, surgery and pensions, and a visitor or mover comparing state-level provision would find Meghālaya's own arrangements unaddressed in the sourced material.

Assessments of police conduct conflict rather than converge. One government-aligned international assessment describes abuse as limited and non-systemic, whereas documented victim interviews record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. Both readings can hold at once across different forces and localities.

New offences attached to the 2026 amendment, including a penalty of up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender, reach beyond the individual trans person to anyone around them, which can affect companions, interpreters, hosts and support workers travelling with a visitor.
localsOnly:
Recognition under the amended law runs through medical certification and district authorities rather than self-declaration, and gender-affirming surgery must be certified by medical boards and district authorities. Residents outside the traditionally recognised groups such as hijra and kinner, and outside the intersex category, fall outside the scheme.

Identity cards are held by only about 32,500 of the 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, so most residents must rely on other documents when dealing with police, railways or airports.

Transition-related healthcare is covered under the Ayushman Bharat scheme, expanded in April 2024 to include all members of the transgender community. Several state governments additionally run welfare boards that coordinate housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and some provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras.

Joint bank accounts and beneficiary designations naming a partner are open to LGBTQ people without restriction, a position the Ministry of Finance clarified in August 2024.

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in force since 2024 omits the gender-identity-specific sexual offences carried by the Indian Penal Code, which changes the protection available to residents reporting sexual violence.

Conversion therapy is banned under the Madras High Court's 7 June 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police and by the National Medical Commission's 2022 order, yet clandestine networks continue to operate.

Intersex infants face non-consensual sex-assignment operations; the Madras High Court ordered the Tamil Nadu government in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material addresses Meghālaya's own policing practices, airport or railway checkpoints, or state welfare schemes for transgender residents. Whether the state runs a welfare board or any facility of the kind operating in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha is unresolved on this inventory.

Whether the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill received presidential assent after late March 2026 is unresolved; the inventory records the measure as passed by Parliament with assent pending.

The relationship between the census figure of 487,803 and the national estimate of around two million transgender people is not reconciled in the sources, and the reasons for the low identity-card count are not stated.

Whether the removal of gender-identity-specific sexual offences from the criminal code has produced a measurable change in reported assaults against trans people is asserted as a fear by trans communities but is not evidenced with figures here.

Enforcement of the Supreme Court's 2021 guidelines and of the National Medical Commission's 2022 conversion-therapy ban, including any prosecutions, is not documented in this inventory.
